title: Powered Exoskeleton for Lifting
body:
A powered exoskeleton is a wearable frame with motors at the hips, knees, and shoulders that multiplies the wearer's strength, letting a worker lift heavy loads, hold tools overhead, and walk long distances with less fatigue.

Real technology context: industrial and medical exoskeletons are in use today, with battery packs, sensors that read the wearer's motion, and motors that add torque where the body needs it; they are heavy, need charging, and work best for repetitive, predictable tasks. Limits: battery life, weight, cost, and the need to fit the wearer's body closely.

Labeled speculative extension: a future full-body exoskeleton that grants superhuman strength all day is fiction, not a product; it would need energy storage, cooling, and joint strength far beyond current hardware, and this record labels that extension as speculative, never as available technology.

title: Myoelectric Prosthetic Arm
body:
A myoelectric prosthetic arm reads electrical signals from the muscles of the remaining limb and turns them into hand and finger movements, letting the wearer grip, hold, and release objects with a prosthetic hand.

Real technology context: modern myoelectric hands offer multiple grip patterns, wrist rotation, and sensory feedback in research models, and they are fitted, trained, and maintained by prosthetists; they are expensive, need charging, and cannot yet match a biological hand's dexterity or touch. Limits: signal noise, weight, and the learning curve of muscle control.

Labeled speculative extension: a prosthetic arm with full human touch, strength, and speed is a research goal, not a product; this record labels that goal as speculative, and it describes only what exists and what is being researched, never a finished superhuman limb.

title: Powered Prosthetic Leg
body:
A powered prosthetic leg uses motors and sensors to bend the knee and push off with the ankle, letting the wearer walk, climb stairs, and run with a gait closer to natural walking than a passive leg allows.

Real technology context: powered knees and ankles are prescribed for active users, with microprocessors adjusting to terrain and speed, and they are fitted by specialists and maintained like machines; they are heavy, costly, and need regular charging. Limits: battery, weight, and the socket's fit against the body.

Labeled speculative extension: a leg that runs faster than any biological leg or jumps over buildings is fiction; this record labels that extension as speculative, and it keeps the real device's benefits, walking and stair climbing, as the honest achievement.

title: Wearable Vision Aid
body:
A wearable vision aid is a headset or glasses system that magnifies, enhances contrast, or reads text aloud for a low-vision wearer, turning the visual world into a form the wearer's remaining vision or hearing can use.

Real technology context: electronic magnifiers, contrast-enhancing glasses, and camera-to-audio readers are sold today, with real benefits for reading, navigation, and face recognition, and real limits of field of view, battery, and cost. Limits: resolution, weight, and the need for training.

Labeled speculative extension: glasses that grant vision through walls or at microscopic scale are fiction; this record labels that extension as speculative, and it describes the aid's real work, making the visible world more usable, as the achievement.

title: Cochlear Implant for Hearing
body:
A cochlear implant is a surgically placed device that bypasses damaged hair cells in the inner ear and stimulates the auditory nerve directly with electrical signals, letting many profoundly deaf recipients perceive sound and, with training, speech.

Real technology context: cochlear implants are a mature medical technology, fitted by surgical and audiology teams, with outcomes that vary by age, duration of deafness, and training; they do not restore normal hearing, and music and noisy rooms remain hard. Limits: surgical risk, cost, and the difference between perceiving sound and hearing naturally.

Labeled speculative extension: an implant that hears whispers across a city or frequencies far beyond human range is fiction; this record labels that extension as speculative, and it treats the implant's real achievement, access to sound and speech, as the honest one.

title: Noninvasive Brain-Computer Interface
body:
A noninvasive brain-computer interface reads brain activity through the scalp, usually with EEG electrodes, and turns patterns of that activity into commands for a cursor, a wheelchair, or a communication device.

Real technology context: EEG interfaces are used in research and in assistive communication, with real but coarse control, a few commands at a time, after training, and they are sensitive to noise, fatigue, and attention. Limits: signal quality through the skull, the small number of reliable commands, and the need for calibration.

Labeled speculative extension: a headset that reads full thoughts or writes memories is fiction; this record labels that extension as speculative, and it describes the interface's real work, a few reliable commands from brain patterns, as the honest achievement.

title: Implanted Brain-Computer Interface (Research)
body:
An implanted brain-computer interface places electrodes on or in the brain to read neural activity with far higher resolution than scalp electrodes, and in research trials it has let participants move robotic arms and type by intention.

Real technology context: implanted interfaces are experimental medical devices in clinical trials, for people with severe paralysis, with surgical risks, infection risks, and long-term stability questions still open; they are not consumer products. Limits: surgery, durability, and the small number of trial participants.

Labeled speculative extension: an implant that grants telepathy, perfect memory, or direct mind-to-mind speech is fiction; this record labels that extension as speculative, and it describes the trial results, cursor control and robotic arms, as the honest, measured achievement.

title: Exosuit for Overhead Work
body:
An exosuit for overhead work is a soft, unpowered or lightly powered harness that supports the arms during overhead tasks, reducing shoulder fatigue for painters, assemblers, and maintenance workers.

Real technology context: passive exosuits use springs and elastic to offload the arms' weight, and they are light, cheap relative to powered frames, and used in factories today; they assist, they do not replace muscle. Limits: they help only for the posture they are tuned to, and they cannot lift loads beyond the wearer's own strength.

Labeled speculative extension: a soft suit that lets a worker hold tons overhead all day is fiction; this record labels that extension as speculative, and it keeps the suit's real benefit, less fatigue in one posture, as the honest claim.

title: Smart Glasses Overlay
body:
Smart glasses overlay information on the wearer's view: directions as arrows on the road, labels on objects, translations of signs, and notifications in the corner of vision, without a hand-held screen.

Real technology context: augmented-reality glasses are sold and piloted for industry, with real benefits for hands-free instructions and remote expert help, and real limits of battery, field of view, brightness outdoors, and weight. Limits: the display's narrow field, the need for network data, and privacy questions about cameras on the face.

Labeled speculative extension: glasses that identify every person, see through walls, or project a full world indistinguishable from reality are fiction; this record labels that extension as speculative, and it describes the overlay's real work, useful labels on the real world, as the achievement.

title: Haptic Gloves for Touch at a Distance
body:
Haptic gloves use vibration, pressure, and resistance to let a wearer feel virtual objects, receive touch feedback from a remote robot, or sense texture in a simulation, adding touch to sight and sound.

Real technology context: haptic gloves are used in virtual reality, teleoperation, and training, with real but coarse feedback, vibration and pressure rather than true texture, and they need calibration and power. Limits: the coarseness of feedback, weight, and cost.

Labeled speculative extension: gloves that let a wearer feel a distant object as if holding it, with full texture, temperature, and weight, are fiction; this record labels that extension as speculative, and it describes the gloves' real feedback, pressure and vibration cues, as the honest achievement.

title: Night-Vision Goggles
body:
Night-vision goggles amplify faint light, or sense heat as infrared, letting a wearer see in darkness where the unaided eye sees nothing, in green-tinted images or thermal color maps.

Real technology context: image-intensifier and thermal goggles are mature technologies used by military, rescue, and wildlife workers, with real limits of resolution, depth perception, field of view, and cost, and they need power and care. Limits: they do not see through walls or in total darkness without an infrared illuminator, and they narrow the wearer's view.

Labeled speculative extension: goggles that see through walls, identify faces at miles, or render night as day are fiction; this record labels that extension as speculative, and it describes the goggles' real work, amplifying faint light and heat, as the achievement.

title: Closed-Circuit Rebreather for Diving
body:
A closed-circuit rebreather recycles the diver's exhaled breath, scrubbing carbon dioxide and adding oxygen, letting a diver stay underwater for hours with almost no bubbles, far longer than an open-circuit tank allows.

Real technology context: rebreathers are used by technical and military divers, with real benefits of duration and silence, and real risks of oxygen toxicity, carbon dioxide buildup, and equipment failure that demand training and maintenance. Limits: complexity, cost, and the need for constant monitoring.

Labeled speculative extension: a device that lets a person breathe underwater unaided, like a fish, is fiction; this record labels that extension as speculative, and it describes the rebreather's real work, recycling breath with machinery, as the honest achievement.

title: High-Altitude Pressure Suit
body:
A high-altitude pressure suit is a sealed garment that keeps a pilot's body pressurized and oxygenated at altitudes where air is too thin to breathe and the body would otherwise fail, as in high-altitude flight and spaceflight.

Real technology context: pressure suits are mature aerospace technology, from early flight suits to modern launch and spacewalk suits, with real limits of bulk, mobility, heat, and cost, and they are maintained as life-support machines. Limits: mobility, cooling, and the suit's own weight.

Labeled speculative extension: a suit that lets a person survive in space unaided, without air, water, or heat, is fiction; this record labels that extension as speculative, and it describes the suit's real work, carrying a livable bubble around a person, as the achievement.

Real technology context: jetpacks have been demonstrated by companies and military trials, with flights measured in minutes and kilometers, and they remain experimental, costly, and dangerous, not a commuting vehicle. Limits: fuel, noise, safety, and regulation.

title: Robotic Assistant Arm
body:
A robotic assistant arm is a mounted multi-joint arm that a user directs by joystick, switch, voice, or brain-computer interface, to grasp, lift, and manipulate objects that the user's own body cannot reach or hold.

Real technology context: assistive arms are prescribed for people with limited arm function, with real benefits of independence in eating, drinking, and handling objects, and real limits of speed, dexterity, weight, and cost. Limits: the arm's speed and the interface's command count.

Labeled speculative extension: an arm that moves with full human speed, strength, and touch, controlled by thought alone without training, is fiction; this record labels that extension as speculative, and it describes the arm's real work, slow and deliberate assistance, as the honest achievement.
